query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using Atom Probe Tomography (APT) with optimized sample preparation to analyze the dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA will reveal that high-temperature oxidation induces near-atomic scale elemental segregation at nanoprecipitate interfaces, which correlates with the formation of protective oxide phases that enhance oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA produced via additive manufacturing with well-dispersed nanoprecipitates in a high-entropy matrix.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled high-temperature oxidation under conditions representative of gas turbine or aerospace operating environments.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environment (e.g., temperatures relevant to gas turbines) with controlled oxygen partial pressure for a fixed exposure duration.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitate interfaces within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: Oxidation drives selective elemental diffusion, leading to the redistribution (segregation) of specific elements (e.g., Ti, Cr) at nanoprecipitate interfaces. This segregation facilitates the nucleation and growth of protective oxide phases that enhance overall oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT measurements will show a measurable enrichment of key elements at the interfaces of nanoprecipitates in the oxidized sample relative to the unoxidized baseline, correlating with improved oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: As-produced (unoxidized) HEA sample characterized by its original near-atomic elemental distribution within nanoprecipitates.
generation.boundary: The observation is limited to the specific HEA composition and processing route; sample preparation artifacts or APT resolution limits in regions with sharp composition gradients may affect the results.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of elemental redistribution and identification of which elements predominantly contribute to protective oxide layer formation remain uncertain and may vary with slight compositional or processing differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples via additive manufacturing. Expose one set to high-temperature oxidation under controlled oxygen atmosphere for a predetermined time and maintain a second set as an unoxidized baseline. Use optimized APT sample preparation to target nanoprecipitate interfaces, and perform three-dimensional compositional mapping.
measurements: Three-dimensional elemental concentration profiles across nanoprecipitate-matrix interfaces.
Comparison of local enrichment of key elements (e.g., Ti, Cr) between oxidized and baseline samples.
Characterization of the thickness and continuity of any formed oxide layers.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT analysis does not reveal statistically significant elemental redistribution or enrichment at nanoprecipitate interfaces in the oxidized sample compared to the baseline, or if such redistribution does not correlate with enhanced oxidation resistance in parallel oxidation performance tests, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Figure 1 shows the typical microstructural evolution of the model SCCPs alloy during stepwise thermo-mechanical processing. The initial as-cast structure of the (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 alloy has a dual-phase structure with bcc (W enriched) and face-centered cubic fcc (Ni-Fe-Ta enriched) phases (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 ). Schematic diagrams of the evolution of its stepwise precipitation process, from the cold-rolled material to the fully processed SCCPs alloy, are shown in Fig. 1a–c . We carefully characterize the evolution of the SCCPs structure in Fig. 1d–i , with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) (details are given in the Methods section). Based on the heavy cold-rolled process, the dislocation density in the material increases sharply (Fig. 1d ), forming high-density dislocation walls (Fig. 1g ), which provide a structural basis for the subsequent stepwise controllable precipitation where the alloy undergoes substantial microstructure evolution during the thermo-mechanical processing, as described as follows:

Microstructure Characterization

Condition (1) was studied here in greater detail using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT). The Condition (1) microstructure is summarized in Fig. 1(a–c) . Annealing at 1200 °C resulted in large, equiaxed grains (grain size = 100 µm [9] ) as seen in the backscattered electron (BSE) SEM image in Fig. 1(a) . A dark-field TEM image, acquired using a {001} superlattice reflection of the B2 phase, is shown in Fig. 1(b) . The [001] zone axis electron diffraction pattern is shown as an inset in the same figure. This dark-field TEM image of Condition (1) revealed a highly-refined microstructure consisting of a two-phase mixture. The highlighted brighter regions, forming the continuous matrix, correspond to the ordered B2 phase while the darker discrete pockets correspond to the disordered BCC phase. The edge-to-edge length of the precipitates (disordered BCC) is ~20 nm and the thickness of the channels (ordered B2) is ~2 nm. The precipitates had a very narrow size distribution and were arranged in regular rows along < 001 > direction. Figure 1 Microstructure of Al 0.5 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0

Microstructure of AlCoFeNi after isothermal annealing at 600 °C and 1000 °C

Samples of the AlCoFeNi alloy were isothermally annealed at either 600 ° C or 1000 ° C for 15 h. Figure 1 shows the back-scatter SEM images of these annealed samples. The samples exhibited a polycrystalline microstructure consisting of large grains. Based on these images the microstructure for both samples appears to be a single phase since no phase separation or second phase precipitation is evident from these SEM images. However, it should be recognized that finer scale second phase precipitates or phase separation may be present in these samples but not revealed at this coarse length scale of imaging. Hence, more detailed investigations have been carried out using TEM and APT. Figure 1 Back-scattered SEM image of AlCoFeNi specimens annealed for 15 h at ( a ) 1000 °C and ( b ) 600 °C.

decision.trend: Earlier high‐entropy alloy studies have pushed the boundaries of strength and oxidation resistance by exploring diverse processing routes – from casting and friction processing to additive manufacturing and thermo‐mechanical treatments – often by tailoring nanoprecipitate distributions. In these works, researchers relied on techniques like TEM, STEM, and EBSD to capture the microstructural evolution and correlate phase distribution with overall properties. More recent studies (e.g., PMC10213035) began incorporating atom-scale techniques such as Atom Probe Tomography (APT) for detailed characterization of coherent precipitates and their interfaces. However, when it comes to elucidating oxidation behavior, the focus has primarily been on bulk oxidation kinetics and formation of protective oxides, rather than resolving the near‐atomic scale elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates under oxidation conditions.
decision.unsolved: The mechanistic details of how nanoprecipitates redistribute elements during high‐temperature oxidation remain unresolved. Conventional imaging and spectroscopy methods do not provide the necessary near-atomic spatial and chemical resolution to directly correlate nanoscale compositional changes with oxidation mechanisms in dual-nanoprecipitation HEA systems.
decision.lever: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) with optimized sample preparation targeting nanoprecipitate interfaces
decision.why: APT offers near-atomic spatial and chemical resolution that can map three-dimensional elemental distributions in nanoprecipitates. This follows the trend wherein recent studies have begun leveraging atom-scale characterization to resolve complex microstructures. Given the gap in understanding the detailed elemental redistribution during oxidation, employing APT is the most plausible next step to mechanistically link nanoprecipitate chemistry with oxidation behavior.
